links.note: The Ramayana and the Mahabharata as great epics, long narrative poems - this concept defines an epic and describes both. Already linked and correct.

The assertion that Makara Sankranti is celebrated with the same name everywhere is false, because this concept's whole point is the map of different names for similar festivals at about the same date. Already linked and correct.
The original Sanskrit Panchatantra against its adaptations - this concept states that one collection of stories has become many, about 200 adaptations in more than 50 languages.

Pairing Sita with the Ramayana against Rama, Krishna and Arjuna misplaced - this concept gives the cast of both epics, Krishna and the Pandavas in one, Rama, Lakshmana, Hanuman, Sita and Ravana in the other.
The Anthropological Survey of India's massive survey called the People of India project - this concept names it. Already linked and correct.

The visible statement is about Pongal and kite flying, which is judged against this concept's map of the harvest festival under its regional names. The item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
The two epics originally composed in Sanskrit - this concept calls them the two Sanskrit epics. Already linked and correct.
Both garments being a length of cloth draped in various styles rests on this concept's account of the sari as a plain, unstitched length of cloth. Already linked and defensible, so left alone.
A mid-January harvest festival with bonfires and feasts is Lohri or Maghi, one of the regional names on this concept's map of the festival that falls on or around January 14.
Patan Patola associated with Gujarat - this concept lists it among the famous silk saris, with Kanjivaram, Banarasi and Muga as the other options.

Ruling out extreme length is decided against this concept's description of the Panchatantra as a collection of delightful stories with animals as main characters that teaches important life skills - the epics, not the Panchatantra, are the long works.

Tribal communities preserving legends connecting their own history with the epics, while the reason about complete adoption without local variation is false because these are retellings. Already linked and correct.
Spotting Paithani as not a West Bengal sari is judged against this concept's list of famous silk saris - Banarasi, Kanjivaram, Paithani, Patan Patola, Muga and Mysore.

The visible claim that Makara Sankranti has one name is refuted by this concept's map of its many regional names. Already linked and correct; the item's other numbered statements are missing from the stem.
The Many in the One - this concept quotes Sri Aurobindo's phrase and the principle of unity in diversity it names, which is what the question asks the reader to interpret.
325 languages counted by the People of India project - this concept's figure. Already linked and correct.
Vincent Smith, the British historian who wondered how a history of India could be written in the face of such bewildering diversity - this concept names him. Already linked and correct.
A relief glossed as a design that stands out from the surface of a panel - the gloss appears in this concept beside the Vaishali stone relief.
Chintz, the printed cotton that became so popular in 17th-century Europe - this concept's box.
Makara Sankranti marking the beginning of the harvest season - this concept's statement. Already linked and correct.
Pongal as the Tamil Nadu name for Makara Sankranti - from this concept's map. Already linked and correct.
Magh Bihu as the Assamese name for the harvest festival around January 14 - from this concept's map of regional names.
The Panchatantra as the collection with animals as main characters that teaches important life skills - this concept's description.
The original Panchatantra text in Sanskrit, at least 2,200 years old - this concept's statement.
An epic as a long poem generally narrating the adventures of heroes and other great figures of the past - this concept's gloss.
Krishna helping the Pandavas against the Kauravas - this concept's summary of the Mahabharata. Already linked and correct.
Ravana kidnapping Sita - this concept's summary of the Ramayana. Already linked and correct.
Hanuman and Lakshmana helping Rama defeat Ravana - this concept names all three. Already linked and correct.
The Bhils, Gonds and Mundas among tribal communities with their own versions of the epics - this concept's list. Already linked and correct.

A tribal shrine in the Nilgiris depicting the five Pandava brothers is an instance of this concept - tribal communities preserving legends that connect their own region with the epic heroes, generally any or all of the five Pandavas.
Saris made mostly of cotton or silk - this concept names both fabrics, and nowadays synthetic ones too.
Sri Aurobindo on the principle of unity in diversity, which has always been normal to India - this concept's second epigraph. Already linked and correct.
